Control theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 12k Articles: 118
Control theory studies how to choose control inputs for a dynamical system so that its plant output follows a reference signal, despite control disturbances and imperfect knowledge of the controlled plant. A controller turns the available information into a control signal. The design must consider both the resulting response and stability theory: a rule that corrects a small mismatch can still produce growing deviations if the interconnection is badly chosen. [ref]
The central distinction is informational. Open-loop control executes planned commands; feedback control uses the measured output of the actual controlled plant to update those commands. A reference signal can describe a destination, while control disturbances describe influences that the controller did not command. A model can predict where the controlled plant should be; measurement tells the controller what actually happened. The authors provide a free full-book PDF through [ref].
For a concrete comparison, all examples below use the same ideal scalar controlled plant:
x˙(t)=u(t)+w(t),y(t)=ym​(t)=x(t),r(t)=1,x(0)=0.
(1)
Here x is an illustrative position, u the control input, w a control disturbance, and ym​ the measured output. Both x and t are dimensionless quantities; the numbers are chosen to expose the mechanism, with no empirical interpretation. The ordinary differential equation says that the present control input and control disturbance accumulate into x. The measured output equals the entire state only in this ideal example; a general plant output need not reveal the entire state.

Plant (control theory)

Words: 209 Articles: 5
Control theory OurBigBook.com
The controlled plant is the part of a control theory model that receives the control input and produces the plant output, including the mechanism that applies the command. The controller is specified separately. In the illustrative ordinary differential equation x˙=u+w, the controlled plant accumulates the control input and control disturbance; it does not itself choose u.

Input (control theory, u(t))

Words: 29
Plant (control theory) OurBigBook.com
A plant input is a signal supplied to the controlled plant. The chosen plant input is its control input; other influences can enter as control disturbances. This use concerns a dynamical system, rather than the input of a computation.

Output (control theory, y(t))

Words: 108 Articles: 2
Plant (control theory) OurBigBook.com
A plant output is a quantity exposed by the controlled plant, often modeled as y=h(x,u,t). In the illustrative model it is y=x. An output of a computation has a different meaning.

Measured output (ym​(t))

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Output (control theory) OurBigBook.com
The measured output is the information about the plant output available to the controller. It may differ from the actual plant output because of measurement noise or feedback delay. In the ideal examples ym​=y=x, so the controller observes the actual current state exactly.
Sensor bias (b=ym​−y)
Words: 45
Measured output OurBigBook.com
A sensor bias is a systematic offset between the measured output and the physical plant output, modeled here as ym​=y+b with constant b. Unlike zero-mean measurement noise, a sensor bias persists when repeated readouts are averaged. A sensor bias affects the physical meaning of a zero tracking error; for a temperature readout, independent thermometer calibration can detect it.

Control disturbance (w(t))

Words: 29
Plant (control theory) OurBigBook.com
A control disturbance is an influence on the controlled plant that is not the chosen control input. In x˙=u+w, a constant w=0.2 increases x by 0.2 per unit t whenever u=0.

Controller (control theory)

Words: 180 Articles: 3
Control theory OurBigBook.com
A controller is the rule or mechanism that chooses a control signal. An open-loop control can depend on a precomputed schedule; a feedback control also uses a measured output and can have its own memory, as in integral action.

Feedback gain (k)

Words: 24
Controller (control theory) OurBigBook.com
A feedback gain sets the strength of a controller's response to its observations. For proportional control, u=ke means that a tracking error e=0.1 produces a control input u=0.2 when k=2.

Actuator saturation (uapplied​=min(umax​,max(umin​,urequested​)))

Words: 75
Controller (control theory) OurBigBook.com
Actuator saturation means the applied control input reaches a device limit even if the controller requests a larger or smaller command. In the heater interpretation, the applied command is bounded between 0 and 100%. If integral action continues accumulating a persistent tracking error beyond that limit, its stored integral can grow without producing the requested physical correction, delaying recovery when the goal changes. The unconstrained steady-state tracking error formulas require that the necessary command can actually be applied. [ref]

PID controller (u(t)=kp​e(t)+ki​∫0t​e(τ)dτ+kd​e˙(t))

Words: 51
Controller (control theory) OurBigBook.com
An ideal PID controller combines proportional control, integral action, and a term proportional to the derivative of the tracking error. With kd​=0, it gives proportional-integral control. The integral stores past error, while the derivative responds to its current rate of change. Practical implementations must account for measurement noise, which an ideal differentiator can amplify. [ref].

Controllability

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Control theory OurBigBook.com
Controllability asks whether the available control inputs can move a dynamical system between every pair of states in its declared state space. Fixing a duration T>0 gives the precise condition RT​(x0​)=X for every x0​∈X, where X is the state space and RT​(x0​) its reachable set. With freely chosen duration, every pair must instead be connectable in some permitted finite time, which may depend on the pair. Always specify admissible control inputs, deadlines and any constraints along the path. [ref]
The surprising part is that one control input can control several state variables by acting at different times. For the double integrator, acceleration changes velocity directly, while the accumulated velocity changes position. Starting from rest, accelerate during the first half of the journey and brake during the second: the final velocity can vanish although the final position has changed. The figure is an analytic mathematical example in dimensionless quantities, with no experimental measurements.
Controllability is useful before trying to design a controller: a requested endpoint outside the reachable set cannot be attained by clever choice of feedback control. The Kalman rank criterion makes this an exact linear algebra calculation for the stated linear time-invariant system model. It concerns whole states, so attaining one plant output is not enough to establish controllability. In quantum control, the declared state space may be an orbit constrained by conservation laws; see quantum controllability and unitary orbit of a density operator.

Controllability matrix (C=[B​AB​⋯​An−1B​])

Words: 65
Controllability OurBigBook.com
For the linear time-invariant system x˙=Ax+Bu, with A∈Rn×n and B∈Rn×m, the controllability matrix has n rows and nm columns. The columns of B are directions influenced directly by the control inputs; AB,A2B,… account for how the dynamics carry their influence into further directions. The column space of the controllability matrix is the zero-state reachable set for any T>0 when inputs are unrestricted. [ref]

Kalman rank criterion (rankC=n)

Words: 131
Controllability OurBigBook.com
For a finite-dimensional continuous-time linear time-invariant system x˙=Ax+Bu on Rn, with constant matrices A,B over the real numbers, no state constraints, and every piecewise continuous function u:[0,T]→Rm allowed as a control input without an amplitude bound, controllability in any fixed T>0 is equivalent to the controllability matrix having rank of a matrix n. The same equivalence holds with all square-integrable functions as inputs. A stronger useful statement is
RT​(x0​)=eATx0​+imC,T>0,
(2)
where eAT is a matrix exponential and imC is the column space. Thus a rank of a matrix r<n leaves only an r-dimensional affine subspace reachable at that time. [ref]
The Kalman rank criterion allows arbitrarily large commands as T shrinks. It does not assert controllability with bounded control inputs, nor test a general nonlinear dynamical system just by counting its inputs. For the double integrator, B=(0,1)T and AB=(1,0)T give two independent directions, despite there being only one control input.

Controllability Gramian (WT​=∫0T​eAsBBTeATsds)

Words: 176
Controllability OurBigBook.com
For T>0 and the constant matrices over the real numbers in the Kalman rank criterion, the finite-time Controllability Gramian accumulates the influence of all command times. Its column space equals that of the controllability matrix, and WT​ is a symmetric positive-definite matrix exactly when the controllability matrix has rank of a matrix n. If so, put δ=x1​−eATx0​. Among square-integrable functions steering x0​ to x1​ at T, the command
u∗​(t)=BTeAT(T−t)WT−1​δ
(3)
minimizes ∫0T​∥u(t)∥2dt, with value δTWT−1​δ. Here T in a matrix superscript denotes transpose. This cost is a squared input norm, not necessarily physical energy, and the optimizing command need not satisfy an amplitude bound. [ref]
For the double integrator, eAsB=(s,1)T, so direct integration gives
WT​=(T3/3T2/2​T2/2T​),detWT​=12T4​>0.
(4)
For a rest-to-rest distance d, u∗​(t)=6d/T2−12dt/T3 and the minimum squared input norm is 12d2/T3. Compare the two constant commands in the double integrator example, whose cost is 16d2/T3: both attain the target, but the smooth command costs less. At T=2, d=1, however, u∗​ peaks at 3/2, so it violates ∣u∣≤1 while the two constant commands remain admissible. Controllability, optimal control, and constrained reachability in control theory answer different questions.

Quantum controllability

Words: 934 Articles: 13
Controllability OurBigBook.com
Quantum controllability concerns the transformations reachable under specified quantum control inputs. Unitary operator controllability concerns entire propagators; density operator controllability concerns conjugation on every spectral orbit; pure-state controllability concerns normalized state vectors or their physical rays. These notions need not coincide.

Bilinear Hamiltonian control system (U˙=−i(H0​+∑k​uk​Hk​)U)

Words: 49
Quantum controllability OurBigBook.com
A finite-dimensional closed quantum control system with fixed drift and control Hermitian matrices, real control inputs, and dynamics linear in the state at fixed controls and affine in the controls at fixed state. Its Dynamical Lie algebra is generated over the reals by iH0​,iH1​,…. Reachability depends on the admissible controls, allowed duration and phase convention.

Dynamical Lie algebra (g=LieR​{iH0​,iH1​,…,iHM​})

Words: 683 Articles: 8
Quantum controllability OurBigBook.com
The dynamical Lie algebra of a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian control system is the real span of its skew-Hermitian drift and control generators and all their nested commutators. The sign choice iH or −iH gives the same algebra. Its connected group determines reachable propagators under the usual freely timed, real-control assumptions. An operator commuting with every generator also commutes with this algebra, imposing invariant sectors.
Connected nondegenerate transition chain generates special unitary control (Lie{iH0​,iH1​}⊇su(N))
Words: 98
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
Let H0​ be diagonal and H1​=∑j=1N−1​dj​(Ej,j+1​+Ej+1,j​), with every dj​=0 and the adjacent absolute energy gaps distinct and nonzero. The squared drift adjoint action has distinct eigenvalues on these coupling components, so Lagrange interpolation isolates every adjacent symmetric coupling. One more commutator gives its antisymmetric partner. Their mutual brackets produce adjacent traceless diagonals, while brackets along the connected chain give all longer-range matrix units. Thus the special unitary Lie algebra is generated. Any nonzero-trace generator also supplies the central direction, giving all of u(N). This is a sufficient condition in the finite-dimensional freely timed real-control model; connectivity alone does not remove frequency degeneracies.
Strongly regular quantum Hamiltonian (∣Ej​−Ek​∣=∣Er​−Es​∣ for distinct transitions)
Words: 57
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
A drift Quantum Hamiltonian is strongly regular when its energy levels are nondegenerate and distinct unordered transitions have distinct absolute nonzero Bohr frequencies. Sometimes regularity is required only on the graph of allowed control transitions. This lets polynomials in the squared drift adjoint action separate different coupling quadratures and permits frequency-selective resonant quantum control. This notion is unrelated to a strongly regular graph.
Codimension-one quantum dynamical algebra is special unitary (dimg=N2−1⟹g=su(N))
Words: 110
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
For N≥2, let g be a Lie subalgebra of u(N) with codimension one. With inner product −Tr(XY) on skew-Hermitian matrices, its orthogonal complement is a line RZ. Invariance of the inner product shows that [X,Z] lies in that line for every X∈g; skew-adjointness of the adjoint action makes [X,Z] orthogonal to Z, hence zero. A nonscalar skew-Hermitian Z has a centralizer of dimension at most (N−1)2+1<N2−1, by its orthogonal eigenspace decomposition, and cannot centralize all of g. Thus Z is scalar and g=su(N). This gives density operator controllability and all determinant-one gates, but not the central phase direction needed for unitary operator controllability.
Symplectic dynamical symmetry in quantum control (XTJ+JX=0⇒UTJU=J)
Words: 118 Articles: 1
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
For a nonsingular skew-symmetric unitary J, if each skew-Hermitian control generator obeys XTJ+JX=0, then so do their real linear combinations and commutators. Differentiating UTJU shows that it stays equal to J. The reachable group is therefore contained in a unitary conjugate of the compact symplectic group. This is preservation of an alternating bilinear form, not commutation with J.
Symplectic invariant of a density operator (IJ​(ρ)=Tr(ρJρTJ†))
Words: 58
Symplectic dynamical symmetry in quantum control OurBigBook.com
For UTJU=J with real orthogonal skew-symmetric J, the dual ρ​=JρTJ† transforms as UρU†​=Uρ​U†. Hence IJ​(ρ) is constant on the reachable unitary orbit of a density operator. Different values can obstruct density operator controllability even when the ordinary spectra agree. For a four-dimensional J pairing indices 1,4 and 2,3, the two diagonal arrangements (a,a,b,b) and (a,b,b,a) have invariants 4ab and 2(a2+b2).
Two adjacent transitions generate the qutrit unitary Lie algebra (LieR​{−iH0​,−iH1​}=u(3))
Words: 84
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
Let H0​=diag(−ω1​,0,−ω2​) and H1​=d1​(E12​+E21​)+d2​(E23​+E32​), with nonzero dj​, distinct positive ωj​. The squared adjoint action of −iH0​ has different eigenvalues −ω12​,−ω22​ on the two adjacent skew-Hermitian couplings. Linear combinations of −iH1​ and its double commutator with −iH0​ isolate both couplings. Further commutators give their real antisymmetric partners, two traceless diagonal generators, and both 1–3 generators, hence the special unitary Lie algebra su(3). The drift has nonzero trace; subtracting its traceless part supplies iI, giving the Lie algebra of the unitary group u(3) and unitary operator controllability under the usual freely timed real-control assumptions.
Orthogonal dynamical symmetry in quantum control (xTJ+Jx=0⇒UTJU=J)
Words: 84
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
Let J be a symmetric unitary matrix and every skew-Hermitian control generator obey xTJ+Jx=0. The condition is closed under real linear combinations and commutators, and evolution preserves UTJU=J. In a unitary basis where J becomes the identity, the generators are real antisymmetric, so the Dynamical Lie algebra is contained in so(N). The state quantity ∣ψTJψ∣ is invariant under the reachable evolution and insensitive to global phase, obstructing unrestricted pure-state controllability. This is a bilinear-form symmetry; it does not assert that J commutes with the Hamiltonians.
Identity augmentation in quantum controllability (g+RiI=u(N),Trg=0⇒g=u(N))
Words: 69
Dynamical Lie algebra OurBigBook.com
For N≥2, suppose a skew-Hermitian Lie algebra becomes all of u(N) after adding the scalar identity direction. Scalar matrices commute, so [g,g]=[u(N),u(N)]=su(N) is contained in g. If g contains any nonzero-trace generator, subtracting its traceless part supplies iI, and g was already all of u(N). This permits using identity-augmented commutator calculations without assuming an additional physical identity control.

Pure-state controllability (Uψ0​=eiχψ1​)

Words: 64
Quantum controllability OurBigBook.com
For freely chosen control duration in a finite-dimensional closed system, pure-state controllability means the reachable group acts transitively on normalized states or their rays. Up to unitary conjugation, the possible Dynamical Lie algebras are u(N), su(N), and for even N=2n the standard compact symplectic Lie algebra sp(n), with or without RiI. For N≥4, the symplectic possibilities are pure-state controllable but generally lack density operator controllability.

Density operator controllability (ρ1​=Uρ0​U†)

Words: 54
Quantum controllability OurBigBook.com
A closed system has density operator controllability when every pair of density operators with the same spectrum can be connected by its controls. Under the standard finite-dimensional Hamiltonian assumptions, this holds exactly for Dynamical Lie algebra u(N) or su(N). This definition ranges over every spectral orbit; a particular degenerate spectrum can be controllable under a smaller group.

Unitary operator controllability (g=u(N))

Words: 54
Quantum controllability OurBigBook.com
A finite-dimensional closed-system control model is unitarily operator controllable when its reachable propagators include every unitary operator. For the usual real Hamiltonian controls and freely chosen duration, this requires the Dynamical Lie algebra to be u(N). If global phase is ignored, su(N) also suffices; exact access to all of U(N) still requires the central phase direction.

Reachability in control theory (x1​∈R(x0​))

Words: 728 Articles: 2
Control theory OurBigBook.com
Reachability in control theory asks about a particular initial state x0​ and target x1​: does some admissible control input make x(T)=x1​ at the declared time T, or at some allowed duration? Controllability requires this for every pair in the declared state space. This is a property of state evolution, distinct from graph reachability.
For a linear time-invariant system, solving the ordinary differential equation by a matrix exponential gives
x(T)=eATx0​+∫0T​eA(T−t)Bu(t)dt.
(5)
The first term is the unforced endpoint. Reachability in control theory asks whether the control input can supply exactly the displacement x1​−eATx0​. The timing matters because the same command is carried by different amounts of subsequent dynamics. [ref]
Here is a contrasting mathematical example with one shared control input:
z˙1​=u,z˙2​=u,A=(00​00​),B=(11​),C=(11​00​).
(6)
The controllability matrix has rank of a matrix one. Since dtd​(z1​−z2​)=0, the difference is invariant under every allowed control input. From (0,0) the reachable set is the diagonal z1​=z2​ when input amplitudes are unrestricted: (1,1) is reachable at T=2 using u=1/2, while (1,0) is impossible at every duration. Having a control input appear in both state equations did not give independent control of both states. This reachable set is pictured alongside the bounded double integrator below.

Reachable set (RT​(x0​)={x(T;x0​,u):u admissible})

Words: 392
Reachability in control theory OurBigBook.com
The reachable set RT​(x0​) collects all endpoints attainable from x0​ at exactly T by admissible control inputs. If arrival any time up to T is allowed, use R≤T​(x0​)=⋃0≤t≤T​Rt​(x0​), with R0​(x0​)={x0​}. These definitions differ: a general dynamical system may drift away after early arrival, so waiting need not preserve the target. The reachable set is always relative to a declared input class and any constraints on the entire path.
For the double integrator starting from (0,0), now require measurable functions as control inputs with ∣u(t)∣≤1 almost everywhere. Write (p,v) for its endpoint at T>0. Two integrals determine the endpoint:
v=∫0T​u(t)dt,p=∫0T​(T−t)u(t)dt.
(7)
Our mathematical example has the exact reachable set
RT​(0)={(p,v):∣v∣≤T,−4T2​+2Tv​+4v2​≤p≤4T2​+2Tv​−4v2​}.
(8)
To see the upper boundary, fix v: put u=1 first and u=−1 last, switching at s=(T+v)/2. This maximizes the weighted integral for position because early commands have the largest weight T−t; the required net velocity fixes s. Formally, (T−t)−(T−s)=s−t has the same sign as this maximizing command, so changing to any other admissible command with the same integral cannot increase p. Reversing the order gives the lower boundary. Pointwise convex combinations of these two commands preserve v and attain every intermediate p, so the formula describes the whole region, not merely a bound. The extreme commands are bang-bang control.
In particular, the bounded double integrator can move from rest to position d and rest again exactly when ∣d∣≤T2/4. Its minimum duration is therefore 2∣d∣​ in these normalized units. With freely chosen time every rest-to-rest distance is attainable; with a fixed deadline many are excluded. Changing the amplitude bound to ∣u∣≤a with a>0 scales this condition to ∣d∣≤aT2/4. This shows why specifying the controls matters even when the Kalman rank criterion gives full rank of a matrix.
In closed quantum control, a density operator reachable set lies inside its unitary orbit of a density operator, since coherent evolution preserves the spectrum. That orbit need not be fully reachable under the available control inputs.

Double integrator (p˙​=v,v˙=u)

Words: 157
Reachability in control theory OurBigBook.com
The double integrator is the linear time-invariant system in which one control input is integrated into velocity, and velocity into position. It is a mathematical idealization of one-dimensional motion under commanded acceleration; for a constant mass m and net force F, Newton's second law gives u=F/m. The worked examples here use normalized dimensionless quantities and assume no control disturbances, rather than describing a laboratory record. [ref]
Writing x=(p,v)T gives
A=(00​10​),B=(01​),C=(01​10​),detC=−1.
(9)
The Kalman rank criterion therefore gives controllability in every T>0 for unrestricted real control inputs. More concretely, choose constants a,b on the first and second halves. Starting at x0​=(p0​,v0​)T, direct integration gives
(p(T)−p0​−Tv0​v(T)−v0​​)=(3T2/8T/2​T2/8T/2​)(ab​).
(10)
The endpoint map has determinant T3/8=0, so these two amplitudes can supply any desired endpoint displacement. For a rest-to-rest move of distance d, take a=4d/T2, b=−4d/T2. At T=2 and d=1 these are the two commands in the first figure. No impulse is needed; shorter deadlines require larger finite commands.

Open-loop control (u(t)=u(t;x0​))

Words: 115
Control theory OurBigBook.com
An open-loop control is prescribed as a function of time, possibly after calculation from an initial state and a dynamical model. It is executed without using observations of the actual current state to change the input. A simulated feedback control law can generate an open-loop waveform, but the resulting laboratory control does not automatically correct errors in the actual state or model.
For the ideal controlled plant with w=0, plan the control input
u(t)={1,0,​0≤t<1,t≥1.​
(11)
Integration gives x(t)=min(t,1), so the planned command reaches the reference signal r=1 at t=1. If an unplanned constant control disturbance w=0.2 begins at t=2, the same open-loop control gives x(t)=1+0.2(t−2) for t≥2: x(4)=1.4 and x(8)=2.2. Knowing the nominal response did not provide a way to correct the actual plant output.

Feedback control selects a control input using observations of the actual controlled plant. In a tracking loop, compare the reference signal r with the measured output ym​ to form the tracking error e=r−ym​, then let the controller change u. The control input changes the plant output, which is measured again: that return path closes the loop. A controller can use earlier observations as well as the latest one. [ref]
For the ideal controlled plant, proportional control u=2(1−x) initially commands u(0)=2. As x approaches 1, the command shrinks. When a positive control disturbance pushes x above 1, the tracking error becomes negative and the control input pushes back. The result is a bounded offset rather than the continuing drift of open-loop control. Integral action can remove that offset by remembering past tracking errors.
A control selected from the observed current state, rather than specified only as a function of the initial state and time. For xt+1​=xt​+ut​ and stage cost xt2​+2xt​ut​+7ut2​, the infinite-horizon feedback ut​=−xt​/3 gives xt​=(2/3)tx0​ and total cost 2x02​. Reference signal (r(t))

Words: 397 Articles: 1
Closed-loop control OurBigBook.com
A reference signal r(t) specifies the desired physical plant output as a function of time. A fixed reference signal is often called a setpoint; a changing reference signal describes a trajectory to follow. A reference signal is a goal, whereas the control input u(t) is the command chosen to achieve that goal. [ref]
Asking for a temperature of 40∘C does not specify a heater command of 40%: dimensional analysis distinguishes the units of these quantities. The reference signal and the measured output must describe the same quantity in the same coordinates before their difference can define a tracking error. An unconverted sensor readout cannot be subtracted directly from a desired temperature.
For example, let y=T−T0​ be temperature rise above a fixed ambient baseline T0​, and write the desired temperature as Td​=T0​+r. A Heaviside step function gives r(t)=R for t≥0, with r(t)=0 before the change: the target rise becomes R at once, although a physical controlled plant generally cannot jump at once. A ramp reference signal r(t)=vt instead asks the temperature rise to increase at a fixed rate v. If R=1∘C and v=0.2∘Cs−1, the first reference signal asks for a lasting one-degree rise; the second asks for a one-degree rise at t=5s and a two-degree rise at t=10s. Here degree Celsius differences are also kelvin differences. A target that grows forever is useful for analytical tests but eventually exceeds a real heater's range.
To make the distinction between a goal and a command concrete, the examples in steady-state tracking error use the first-order low-pass filter as a new controlled plant, rather than the accumulating controlled plant x˙=u+w used in the earlier feedback demonstration:
τy˙​+y=Ku+d,τ>0,K>0.
(12)
The time constant τ has units of time, K has units of plant output per control input, and the additive control disturbance d has the units of y. This d is an equivalent output offset, not the rate-like w in x˙=u+w. A heater interpretation uses y in degree Celsius differences and u in percentage points of heater command, with K in degrees per percentage point; the control input is a command, not a direct measurement of delivered power. With exact measurement, holding y=R requires u=(R−d)/K. Thus even a constant reference signal can require a persistent nonzero control input. The numerical model below is deliberately synthetic and has no fitted laboratory parameters.

Tracking error (e(t)=r(t)−ym​(t))

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Closed-loop control OurBigBook.com
The tracking error used by the controller is the signed difference
e(t)=r(t)−ym​(t),
(13)
between the reference signal and the measured output. A positive tracking error means the readout is below the desired value; a negative tracking error means it is above. With exact measurement ym​=y, r=1 and y=1.1 give e=−0.1. For a positive-response controlled plant, positive feedback gain in proportional control u=kp​e then reduces the plant output. The sign of the controller must also account for the sign of the controlled plant's response: a positive command that reduces the plant output requires a different sign choice. Kantor uses the opposite tracking error convention, PV−SP, together with a minus sign in his controller; translating both signs gives the convention here. [ref]
Distinguish the controller's tracking error from the physical plant output discrepancy ε=r−y. If the readout has constant sensor bias b, then
ym​=y+b,e=ε−b,ε=e+b.
(14)
All four quantities r,y,ym​,e have the same units under dimensional analysis; a sensor bias is expressed in those units too. A readout that is too high by 0.2∘C can make e=0 when the physical temperature is 0.2∘C below the goal. Integral action integrates the tracking error it receives; it cannot infer this missing calibration information from that tracking error alone. Thermometer calibration against an independent reference addresses a different problem from tuning a feedback gain.
A motivating apparatus/model comparison is Park, Martin, Kelly and Hedengren's temperature-control laboratory: two TIP31C heaters with attached TMP36GZ sensors and heat sinks, an Arduino, a power supply, and a USB-connected computer. The readout converts sensor voltage to temperature; software records that measured output while specifying heater commands from 0 to 100%. For the single-heater test, one command changes in steps and the other heater stays off. Parameters are fitted to one run, then a different command sequence tests predictions without feeding measured temperatures into the simulation. The authors observe that their richer thermal model predicts the response better than the approximation with a single time constant and a delayed control input, especially after command changes. The real sensor has its own thermal lag. They also repeat the same command profile at different ambient temperatures and find changes in the response, motivating ambient-condition reporting. This experiment measures a command-to-readout response, not independently the exact heater temperature or delivered power. [ref]
The lesson for tracking error is to record three traces during a tracking test: the reference signal, the measured output, and the applied control input. Their first difference is the tracking error; a model prediction minus a readout is instead a model discrepancy. In a proposed comparison of proportional control and proportional-integral control, keep the initial temperature, ambient conditions, heater limits, and target changes fixed; run the second heater separately as a known control disturbance. Independent thermometer calibration is needed to assess physical accuracy. These are suggested controls, not additional experiments claimed for the paper. A sensor's lag, measurement noise, actuator saturation, and changed ambient conditions can all invalidate conclusions drawn from the ideal first-order model.

The steady-state tracking error is

(15)
when this finite limit exists. A finite steady-state tracking error does not require the reference signal, the plant output, or the control input to become constant: all can grow while their difference settles. If the tracking error grows without bound or keeps oscillating, report that behavior rather than assigning a finite steady-state tracking error. Eventual accuracy and asymptotic stability are different questions.
For the first-order low-pass filter τy˙​+y=Ku+d introduced in reference signal, assume exact measurement, constant control disturbance d, and no actuator saturation or feedback delay. Under proportional control u=kp​(r−y) with kp​>0, a constant reference signal r=R gives

(16)
The decaying homogeneous solution has rate (1+Kkp​)/τ>0, so this equilibrium point is approached from any finite initial condition. A nonzero tracking error is needed to maintain the control input that balances the model's tendency to relax toward y=d. This differs from the accumulating controlled plant x˙=u+w, for which proportional control already tracks a constant reference signal exactly when w=0. The presence or absence of a step offset depends on both the controlled plant and the controller.
For a ramp reference signal r=vt, the same proportional control gives
τe˙+(1+Kkp​)e=τv+vt−d.
(17)
Its long-time particular solution grows with slope v/(1+Kkp​) when v=0. Thus the controlled plant and homogeneous closed-loop response are stable, but the tracking error has no finite steady-state tracking error. A changing goal requires a different performance test from a fixed destination.
Now use proportional-integral control u=kp​e+ki​z, z˙=e, with ki​>0. For the same controlled plant, differentiate the error equation on intervals where the inputs are smooth:

The characteristic polynomial τλ2+(1+Kkp​)λ+Kki​ has both roots of a polynomial in the open left half-plane: real roots have negative sum and positive product, and a nonreal complex conjugate pair has negative real part. This proves decay of the homogeneous error for this model. It does not prove stability of an arbitrary controlled plant controlled by positive gains. At a reference jump, use the original ordinary differential equations to set the new initial conditions, rather than treating the reference as smooth at that jump.
With a constant reference signal and constant control disturbance, proportional-integral control therefore gives ess​=0. At its equilibrium point, y∗​=R, u∗​=(R−d)/K, and z∗​=(R−d)/(Kki​). The stored integral maintains the required command while the current tracking error vanishes. For a ramp reference signal, however, the forcing above is v, and
ess​=Kki​v​.
(19)
The tracking error settles even though the accumulated integral and the required control input grow. This finite offset is the error needed to keep increasing that command. For r=at2/2 with a=0, the forcing is τa+at and even this proportional-integral control leaves a tracking error growing with slope a/(Kki​). Choose τ=2s, K=1∘C per percentage point, kp​=1 percentage point per degree, and ki​=0.5 percentage points per degree-second. Thus Kkp​=1 is dimensionless, and Kki​=0.5s−1. In the following formulas, t denotes the numerical time in seconds and y,e,r denote numerical temperature rises in degrees. For the unit-step reference signal r=1, proportional control and proportional-integral control respectively give
yP​(t)=21​(1−e−t),eP​(t)=21​(1+e−t),uP​(t)=eP​(t);
(20)
yPI​(t)=1−e−t/2,ePI​(t)=e−t/2,uPI​(t)=1.
(21)

yP​(t)=0.1(t−1+e−t),eP​(t)=0.1(t+1−e−t),uP​(t)=eP​(t);

Substitution into 2y˙​+y=u and into the controller equations checks these solutions without invoking an unverified limiting rule. The proportional control step offset is 0.5 degrees; the proportional-integral control step offset is zero. The proportional control ramp error grows; the proportional-integral control ramp offset is 0.4 degrees, exactly v/(Kki​).
The conclusions have specific limits. With constant sensor bias b, stable proportional-integral control for a feasible constant reference signal drives the measured tracking error to zero but leaves the physical discrepancy εss​=b. Under proportional control, the measured offset instead becomes (R−b−d)/(1+Kkp​). If actuator saturation prevents the required control input, zero step offset is not achievable by these formulas. A changing control disturbance contributes −d˙ to the error equation, while feedback delay can change stability; neither is covered by the constant-disturbance result. These restrictions are what make steady-state tracking error useful: it identifies the input, measurement convention, and model for which an accuracy claim is actually justified.

For w=0.2, doubling the feedback gain from k=2 to k=4 reduces the offset from 0.1 to 0.05. This improvement is a statement about the ideal model: it neglects feedback delay and measurement noise, so it does not establish that arbitrarily large feedback gains are safe. [ref]

Proportional-integral control is the proportional and integral part of a PID controller, with the derivative term omitted. Proportional-integral control combines proportional control with integral action. For the ideal controlled plant, a constant reference signal, exact measurement and a constant control disturbance, the ordinary differential equations give

(26)
The characteristic polynomial is λ2+kp​λ+ki​. Positive kp​ and ki​ imply asymptotic stability of the equilibrium point: real roots of a polynomial have negative sum and positive product, hence are both negative; a nonreal complex conjugate pair has real part −kp​/2<0. This is a short stability check for this ideal controlled plant, rather than a rule for every dynamical system.
At the equilibrium point, e∗​=0, x∗​=r, and z∗​=−w/ki​. For w=0.2 and ki​=1, the stored value z∗​=−0.2 supplies u∗​=−0.2 even though the tracking error is zero. This separates the eventual accuracy from the transient response: integral action cancels the lasting offset but can make the plant output pass beyond the goal. The authors discuss practical limits on integral action in Åström and Murray, Feedback Systems, Chapter 11.
For kp​=2, ki​=1, x(0)=z(0)=0 and w=0, the characteristic polynomial is (λ+1)2. The initial conditions are e(0)=1 and e˙(0)=−2, giving

For positive feedback delay τ, an initial condition at a single instant is insufficient. Prescribe a continuous function ϕ throughout [−τ,0]: for 0≤t≤τ, the derivative depends on x(t−τ)=ϕ(t−τ). A right derivative at t=0 is understood; the earlier history need not itself obey the subsequent control law. Once this first interval is computed, it supplies the delayed values for the next interval. This successive integration is the method of steps for a delay differential equation. [ref]
For the constant initial history of delayed feedback ϕ(t)=1, direct integration gives
x(t)=1−kt(0≤t≤τ),x(t)=1−kt+2k2​(t−τ)2(τ≤t≤2τ).
(30)
For k=1, τ=1.2, the plant output crosses zero at t=1, while its measured output remains positive until t=2.2. At t=1.4, the delayed command therefore increases the magnitude of the actual deviation. This short exact calculation explains the first diagram without relying on a numerical approximation.

Delay stability of proportional integrator control (kτ<π/2)

Words: 462
Feedback delay OurBigBook.com
For the constant-coefficient model x′(t)=−kx(t−τ) with k>0 and τ≥0, the zero equilibrium point is asymptotically stable if and only if kτ<π/2. For positive τ, perturbations are measured by the supremum norm of the initial history of delayed feedback; in the stable regime, every continuous history produces a solution tending to zero. At equality, nondecaying sinusoids prevent asymptotic stability. For kτ>π/2, growing oscillatory solutions exist. These statements concern this ideal linear time-invariant system, rather than an arbitrary controlled plant. The corresponding linear equation and its threshold are developed in Cain and Reynolds, section 6.4, pages 174–177.
Substitute the exponential function x(t)=est, allowing a complex number s. The characteristic equation is
s+ke−sτ=0.
(31)
For positive feedback delay this is not a characteristic polynomial: it has infinitely many roots. A root's real part determines growth or decay of its exponential mode, and its imaginary part determines the angular frequency. To find the first boundary, set s=iω with ω>0 and use Euler's formula:
kcos(ωτ)=0,ω−ksin(ωτ)=0.
(32)
The smallest positive crossing is ω=k and ωτ=π/2. Thus at τc​=π/(2k) the complex conjugate roots are s=±ik. In fact, with the matching initial history of delayed feedback,
x(t)=Acos(kt)+Bsin(kt)
(33)
solves the delay differential equation exactly: a quarter-cycle feedback delay turns the past displacement into precisely the current derivative. Its cycle lasts 2π/k=4τc​. The amplitude is arbitrary; this linear model does not select a finite-amplitude oscillation.
The roots cross toward growth as feedback delay increases. Differentiating the characteristic equation at fixed k gives
dτds​=−1+sτs2​,Re(dτds​)s=ik,τ=τc​​=1+(π/2)2k2​>0.
(34)
This calculation identifies the direction of the first destabilization. The full threshold also requires ruling out earlier unstable roots: if s=α+iβ with α≥0 and β>0, the characteristic equation implies cos(βτ)≤0 and 0<β≤k, hence kτ≥βτ≥π/2. A real nonnegative root is impossible because s+ke−sτ>0 there. This supplies the geometric reason the threshold is a quarter-cycle rather than an arbitrary fitting constant.
The tradeoff is concrete. Without feedback delay, increasing k shortens the exponential decay time constant 1/k. With known τ>0, the same proportional control must satisfy k<π/(2τ). For τ=0.2s, the threshold is k≈7.854s−1: k=5s−1 is stable and k=8s−1 is unstable. A design close to the boundary leaves little room for additional feedback delay; reducing k or reducing measurement latency increases that room. The zero-delay time constant is only a comparison scale, not the decay time of the delayed response. Frank discusses the gain–delay compromise in Control Theory Tutorial, section 13.4 and figure 13.3.

Delayed cursor feedback experiment

Words: 212
Feedback delay OurBigBook.com
Can feedback delay change correction timing even when the physical task stays the same? Susilaradeya and colleagues tested this in a human tracking experiment. Participants pressed with both index fingers against fixed force sensors; the two forces controlled a screen cursor along two diagonal axes. A target moved in slow circular motion, usually at 0.2 rotations per second. The researchers sampled the forces at 50 samples per second and inserted an additional delay of 0, 100, 200, 300, or 400 milliseconds before displaying the cursor. Each trial lasted 20 seconds; the 70 trials included 14 per delay, in pseudorandom order. [ref]
The readout was fluctuation in cursor angular velocity, analyzed by Fourier transforms over approximately 10 seconds from the middle of each trial. The principal peak was around 2 hertz without added delay, around 1.4 hertz with 100 milliseconds, and around 1 hertz with 200 milliseconds. Thus changing observation timing changed the timing of corrective motion. [ref] This is an empirical motivation for taking stale observations seriously. Human feedback control includes prediction and other dynamics; these observations do not measure k in the ideal integrator model or test its kτ=π/2 boundary.

Choosing those parameters can make a prescribed pure state stationary and globally attractive. At exceptional parameter values, the dissipator can instead leave an entire family of states stationary, so algebraic target stationarity does not establish stabilization. Checking the Affine Bloch equation and its transverse eigenvalues distinguishes these possibilities.

A controlled Markov process has transition probabilities or rates depending on its current state and the chosen control action. A Markov policy selects an action from the current state and possibly the time. Once such a policy is fixed, the induced state evolution is a Markov process. For general history-dependent controls, the state alone need not remain Markov. A dynamic programming operator optimizes over the available actions at each state.
Markov decision process
Words: 67
Controlled Markov process OurBigBook.com
A Markov decision process specifies states, admissible actions, action-dependent transition probabilities and rewards. A policy chooses actions from observed information; a time-homogeneous problem uses transition and reward rules independent of the date. A Bellman equation optimizes current reward plus the conditional value of subsequent decisions. For nonnegative rewards, finite-horizon values increase as the horizon grows, while identification of their limit with the infinite-horizon value requires an approximation argument for admissible policies.

The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation becomes a variational inequality with a constraint on directional derivatives of the value function.

State estimation

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Control theory OurBigBook.com
State estimation infers an unobserved state of a dynamical system from its observations and a model of its evolution. An observed position can help estimate an unobserved velocity; repeated noisy observations can help distinguish changes in the state from measurement noise. The result should describe both an estimate and its uncertainty. A Kalman filter does this exactly for a linear Gaussian state-space model, maintaining a conditional expectation and conditional covariance.
The time at which information is available matters. Causal state filtering estimates the present state from observations available now. State prediction estimates a future state from those same observations. Later observations can improve an estimate of a past state, but that is a different information set from the one a live controller had. Kalman explicitly distinguishes these estimation tasks in A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems (1960), section Optimal Estimates.

Causal state filtering (E[xt​∣y1​,…,yt​])

Words: 33
State estimation OurBigBook.com
Causal state filtering estimates the current state of a dynamical system from observations up to the current time. Under quadratic loss, the conditional expectation is an optimal estimate. A Kalman filter obtains this estimate recursively for a linear Gaussian state-space model, without using future observations.

State prediction (E[xt+1​∣y1​,…,yt​])

Words: 36
State estimation OurBigBook.com
State prediction estimates a future state of a dynamical system using observations already available. A state-space model supplies the transition law. Unlike causal state filtering at the next time, the prediction has not yet incorporated that next observation; a Kalman prediction step therefore includes uncertainty from new process noise.

Process noise (wt​,Qt​=Cov(wt​))

Words: 45
State estimation OurBigBook.com
Process noise is the random contribution to a state transition in a state-space model. It represents uncertainty in how the state evolves. Measurement noise instead affects the observed value of the state. In the local-level state-space model xt​=xt−1​+wt​, yt​=xt​+vt​, the first disturbance changes the state itself; the second changes its measurement.

Words: 58
State estimation OurBigBook.com
A best affine state estimate minimizes mean squared error among estimates a+Cy formed from the available observation vector y. With finite second moments and invertible observation covariance matrix, it is
x=E[x]+Cov(x,y)Cov(y)−1(y−E[y]).
(35)
This follows from the orthogonal projection of centered state components onto the linear span of centered observation components. For Jointly Gaussian state and observation it equals the conditional expectation; for general laws a nonlinear estimate can have lower mean squared error.

Kalman filter (mt​=mt−​+Kt​(yt​−Ht​mt−​))

Words: 1k Articles: 9
State estimation OurBigBook.com
The Kalman filter alternates a Kalman prediction step with a Kalman measurement update. It carries a state estimate forward using a state-space model, then adjusts it by the part of the new observation that was not predicted: the innovation. The Kalman gain determines the adjustment from the uncertainty of the prediction and the measurement noise. A noisy measurement should have less influence than an equally surprising precise one.
For a precise discrete-time statement, let the state and observation be vectors in real vector spaces obeying the linear state-space model
xt​=At​xt−1​+Bt​ut−1​+wt​,yt​=Ht​xt​+vt​.
(36)
The matrices and control inputs are known. Assume a Gaussian random vector x0​ with mean m0​ and covariance matrix P0​, and mutually independent centered Gaussian noises wt​,vt​, independent of x0​, with covariance matrices Qt​,Rt​. Suppose Rt​ is positive-definite, so the observation innovation covariance is invertible. Then the recursions below give the exact posterior mean mt​=E[xt​∣y1​,…,yt​] and posterior covariance matrix Pt​, hence the full conditional multivariate normal distribution. They also minimize mean squared error. Without the Gaussian assumptions, suitable second-order assumptions still give best affine state estimates, but do not generally give an exact posterior distribution. [ref].
For an exact scalar example, suppose the predicted state has normal distribution N(10,4) and a measurement reports y=14 in the same units. With measurement noise variance R=1, the Kalman gain is 4/(4+1)=4/5 and the posterior distribution is
x∣y=14∼N(13.2,0.8).
(37)
With the same prediction and observed value but measurement noise variance R=16, the Kalman gain becomes 1/5 and the posterior distribution is instead N(10.8,3.2). Both updates move toward the observation; the more precise measurement moves the estimate further and reduces uncertainty more.
The useful compression is exact under the stated model: the two objects mt​,Pt​ contain everything from the past observations needed for the next update. Their size depends on the state dimension, not on the length of the observation history. This makes causal state filtering practical when observations arrive continually. It also gives Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control an estimate of the state on which to act.
Rudolf E. Kalman's 1960 paper organized linear filtering around state transitions, error covariance and recursive computation, connecting estimation with optimal regulation. Its introduction acknowledges earlier work by Wiener, Bode, Shannon and others; the useful historical claim is this particular formulation, rather than that estimation began in 1960. [ref].

The Kalman prediction step advances the previous posterior mean and posterior covariance matrix through the state transition:
mt−​=At​mt−1​+Bt​ut−1​,Pt−​=At​Pt−1​At⊤​+Qt​.
(38)
The minus superscript marks information before observing yt​. The transpose and matrix multiplication propagate the old uncertainty; Qt​ adds the uncertainty of the new process noise. A known control input changes the mean but contributes no additional variance. If the control input itself is uncertain, that uncertainty needs its own model.

This includes uncertainty in both the predicted state and the measurement noise. It is a covariance in observation coordinates; Pt−​ is a covariance in state coordinates, and need not even have the same dimensions.

For a scalar state observed directly, it reduces to K=P−/(P−+R). With positive variances, 0<K<1, and the Kalman measurement update is the weighted mean (1−K)m−+Ky. That interpretation belongs to the scalar unit-coefficient case; a general Kalman gain is a rectangular matrix, not a collection of weights necessarily between zero and one.

The posterior covariance matrix subtracts a positive semidefinite matrix, reflecting the information supplied by the measurement. Even if the innovation is zero and the mean does not move, the uncertainty can decrease. In this linear Gaussian model the posterior covariance matrix depends on the observation geometry and its uncertainty, rather than on the numerical observed value.
The derivation is one application of Gaussian conditional expectation per measurement. Before observing yt​, the state and observation have joint covariance matrix

(42)
Conditioning the upper block on the lower block gives exactly the two update equations. The upper-right block explains the Kalman gain: a measured component corrects a state component only to the extent that their prediction errors have covariance. The measurement can therefore improve an unobserved velocity when a state-space model correlates its error with an observed position.

The observation innovation variance is Vt​=FGPt−1​G⊤F⊤+FQF⊤. Omitting the second term incorrectly removes the current process noise. For a concrete example with two state components that are dimensionless quantities, take predicted mean (10,0)⊤, predicted covariance matrix
R=(42​29​),
(43)
and exact observation of the first component, F=(1,0), X=12. The innovation is 2, its variance is 4, and the Kalman gain is (1,1/2)⊤. The posterior mean and posterior covariance matrix are therefore
m=(121​),P=R−41​(42​)(4​2​)=(00​08​).
(44)
The observed component now has zero variance. The second component remains uncertain, but its posterior mean changes and its variance falls from 9 to 8 because its prediction error had nonzero correlation with that of the first. This is the mechanism by which measurements of one component can inform another.

For the state-space model St​=GSt−1​+wt​, Xt​=FSt​+vt​, assume independent Gaussian process noise and measurement noise of variances W,V, independent of the prior state and previous observations. A normal distribution for the filtered state, with mean m and variance P, predicts mean Gm and variance R=G2P+W. Here R denotes predicted state variance, rather than the observation-noise covariance notation used in the vector equations above. Gaussian conditional expectation then gives posterior mean Gm+K(X−FGm) and posterior variance RV/(F2R+V), where the Kalman gain is K=FR/(F2R+V).
Mere weak white noise assumptions do not imply normal posterior distributions: independent process noise with a Rademacher distribution makes the next state a mixture of two shifted normal distributions. The Kalman filter can still describe a best affine state estimate under appropriate second-order assumptions, but that is distinct from an exact Gaussian conditional law.

The nonnegative root lies below one for finite c>0; it tends to zero with c and to one as c grows. Thus noisier state evolution assigns more weight to the latest observation.

Words: 255
Kalman filter OurBigBook.com
Consider a local-level state-space model xt​=xt−1​+wt​, yt​=xt​+vt​, with mutually independent centered Gaussian noises of variances Q=1/4 and R=1. Start with x0​∼N(10,4), independently of these noises. Before the first observation, the Kalman prediction step gives m1−​=10, P1−​=17/4. If y1​=14, the Kalman gain is 17/21, and the posterior mean and posterior variance become
m1​=10+2117​(14−10)=21278​,P1​=2117​.
(47)
The next Kalman prediction step keeps the mean m2−​=278/21 but adds fresh process noise variance, giving P2−​=89/84. If y2​=12, then
K2​=17389​,m2​=21278​+17389​(12−21278​)=1732180​,P2​=17389​.
(48)
Thus new uncertainty is introduced at each transition and reduced by each measurement. It does not shrink to zero merely because many measurements have arrived: the state continues to change.
The steady-state local-level Kalman gain here is
K∞​=817​−1​≈0.390388.
(49)
With R=1, the limiting posterior variance has the same numerical value. By contrast, the static-state model Q=0 with P0​=4 gives Pt​=1/(t+1/4) and Kt​=1/(t+1/4). That decreasing gain is appropriate for a state that truly remains constant. Applied to the changing random walk, it builds confidence in the wrong model. The choice of process noise is therefore a statement about state evolution, rather than just an instruction to make a plot look smoother.

Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control

Words: 100 Articles: 2
Control theory OurBigBook.com
Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control combines a linear system, Gaussian uncertainty, a quadratic cost, and feedback based on a Kalman filter state estimate.

Terminal-position reduction of double-integrator control (z=x+(T−t)y,u∗​=−1+(T−t)3/3(T−t)z​)

Words: 53
Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control OurBigBook.com
For dx=ydt, dy=udt+dW and terminal cost x(T)2 plus running cost u2, the displayed change of state gives dz=(T−t)udt+(T−t)dW. A quadratic value function has coefficient P(t)=[1+(T−t)3/3]−1 and additive noise cost log[1+(T−t)3/3]. Minimizing its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation gives the displayed control. The gain is unchanged if the additive noise is removed, illustrating certainty equivalence.

Separation principle

Words: 29
Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control OurBigBook.com
In a linear-quadratic-Gaussian control problem, the optimal control applies the full-information linear-quadratic feedback law to the conditional state estimate. The control gain is independent of the state-estimation error covariance.

Continuous Lyapunov equation (AX+XAT+Q=0)

Words: 34
Control theory OurBigBook.com
The continuous Lyapunov equation is AX+XAT+Q=0. If every eigenvalue of A has negative real part, it has a unique solution for each Q, and a positive-definite Q gives a positive-definite X.

Transfer function (G(s)=Y(s)/U(s))

Words: 981 Articles: 6
Control theory OurBigBook.com
A transfer function packages the response of a linear time-invariant system into a rule for turning a plant input into a plant output. Instead of solving a differential equation separately for every signal, take a Laplace transform, multiply by G(s), then transform back. This also makes it possible to compare slow and fast oscillations through the continuous-time frequency response.
Here consider a continuous-time, causal, finite-dimensional linear time-invariant system with one plant input u(t) and one plant output y(t). With every initial state set to zero, its transfer function is defined by
U(s)=L{u}(s),Y(s)=L{y}(s),Y(s)=G(s)U(s).
(50)
The ratio G(s)=Y(s)/U(s) is used where U(s)=0 in a common Laplace convergence region; G describes the system, independently of that particular plant input. Zero initial state matters: stored motion or another nonzero initial condition can contribute to the plant output even when the plant input vanishes. [ref]
The first-order low-pass filter below shows the same transfer function predicting both a step and a sustained sinusoid. Its pole gives a decay rate, its value at zero gives the eventual gain, and its values along the imaginary axis give the continuous-time frequency response. These descriptions make a useful bridge between a physical relaxation model and control theory calculations.

First-order low-pass filter (G(s)=K/(τs+1))

Words: 281
Transfer function OurBigBook.com
A first-order low-pass filter with positive constant gain K and time constant τ>0 obeys the ordinary differential equation
τy′(t)+y(t)=Ku(t).
(51)
The derivative term limits how quickly the plant output follows a changing plant input. A larger time constant means slower adjustment. This standard form, with K=1, is developed in Derek Rowell, MIT 2.004, lecture 20, section 1.1: first-order systems; the following calculation keeps the gain K explicit.
Write y0​=y(0). The Laplace transform of the derivative is sY(s)−y0​, so
τ(sY(s)−y0​)+Y(s)=KU(s),Y(s)=τs+1K​U(s)+τs+1τy0​​.
(52)
Setting the initial condition y0​=0 gives the transfer function G(s)=K/(τs+1). Its single simple pole is s=−1/τ, which has negative real part. The unforced response decays, and the input/output map has BIBO stability. The eventual gain for a constant plant input is G(0)=K.
For a unit step, represented by the Heaviside step function u(t)=H(t), the Laplace transform is U(s)=1/s. From zero initial condition,
Y(s)=s(τs+1)K​=sK​−s+1/τK​,y(t)=K(1−e−t/τ)(t≥0).
(53)
Take K=2 and τ=3s, with dimensionless plant input and plant output. Then y(t)=2(1−e−t/(3s)) rises toward 2. After one time constant, at t=3s, it reaches 2(1−e−1)≈1.2642, or 63.2% of its final value. At t=9s=3τ, it reaches 2(1−e−3)≈1.9004, or 95.0%. These percentages describe the rise from zero, rather than an instantaneous jump to the target.
With a nonzero initial condition, the same step instead gives
y(t)=K(1−e−t/τ)+y0​e−t/τ.
(54)
For K=2 and τ=3s, compare y0​=0 with y0​=1. Their plant outputs differ by e−t/(3s) despite having the same transfer function and the same plant input. The extra exponential decay term must be supplied from the initial condition; G and u alone cannot determine it.

Continuous-time frequency response (G(iω))

Words: 293 Articles: 1
Transfer function OurBigBook.com
The continuous-time frequency response is the frequency response of a continuous-time linear time-invariant system. From zero initial state, a BIBO stable system driven by a sustained sinusoid u(t)=Acos(ωt) approaches the steady response
yss​(t)=A∣G(iω)∣cos(ωt+argG(iω)).
(55)
Any decaying initial or switching transient is separate. The modulus ∣G(iω)∣ is the amplitude gain; the complex argument is the shift in oscillation phase. Thus evaluating a transfer function at s=iω measures both how much of an oscillation passes through and how far it lags.
For the first-order low-pass filter, with K>0, direct complex number arithmetic gives
G(iω)=1+iωτK​,∣G(iω)∣=1+(ωτ)2​K​,argG(iω)=−arctan(ωτ).
(56)
The phase uses the inverse tangent branch between −π/2 and π/2. Low angular frequencies have gain close to K and little lag. High angular frequencies have gain approximately K/(ωτ) and lag approaching π/2. This is why the model is a first-order low-pass filter: it suppresses fast variation compared with slow variation. Rowell relates frequency response gain and phase to poles and then introduces Bode plots in MIT 2.004, lecture 32, sections 1 and 2.
At the corner angular frequency,
ωc​=τ1​,∣G(iωc​)∣=2​K​,argG(iωc​)=−4π​.
(57)
For K=2 and τ=3s, ωc​=1/3rads−1, the gain is 2​≈1.4142, and the lag is 45 degrees. The angular frequency ω is measured in radians per second; ordinary frequency f is measured in hertz (cycles per second), with ω=2πf. Consequently the same corner is fc​=1/(2πτ)≈0.0531Hz, not 1/3Hz.

Bode plot

Words: 46
Continuous-time frequency response OurBigBook.com
A Bode plot displays the gain and oscillation phase of a frequency response against a logarithmic frequency axis. Gain is often shown as 20log10​∣G(iω)∣ in decibels; phase can use degrees or radians. The first-order low-pass filter loses approximately 20 decibels per factor of ten in angular frequency well above its corner. [ref]

Proper rational transfer function (G(s)=N(s)/D(s),degN≤degD)

Words: 44
Transfer function OurBigBook.com
A proper rational transfer function is a rational function whose numerator polynomial has polynomial degree no greater than its denominator polynomial, after common factors are canceled. Every finite-dimensional continuous-time linear time-invariant system of the form x˙=Ax+Bu, y=Cx+Du has such a transfer function G(s)=C(sI−A)−1B+D. [ref]

Bounded-input bounded-output stability

Words: 152
Transfer function OurBigBook.com
Bounded-input bounded-output stability means that every bounded plant input produces a bounded plant output from zero initial state. For a causal continuous-time linear time-invariant system with a proper rational transfer function, BIBO stability is equivalent to every pole of the reduced transfer function having strictly negative real part. Cancel common factors first: an apparent denominator root may be absent from the reduced transfer function. For K/(τs+1) with τ>0, the only pole is −1/τ, so the first-order low-pass filter is BIBO stable. [ref]
Internal asymptotic stability also requires every unforced internal state to decay. A canceled factor can hide a growing internal state. For example, consider the linear system of ordinary differential equations
x˙1​=−x1​+u,x˙2​=x2​+u,y=x1​.
(58)
Its zero-state transfer function can be written (s−1)/((s+1)(s−1))=1/(s+1) and has BIBO stability. Yet from zero initial conditions and a unit-step plant input, x2​(t)=et−1 grows without bound while the plant output remains bounded. The reduced transfer function conceals that second state. Even a transfer function with no visible cancellations can be implemented with additional hidden states; its poles alone do not establish internal asymptotic stability of an arbitrary implementation.

Nyquist stability criterion

Words: 38
Transfer function OurBigBook.com
Let L be the open-loop transfer function. The winding of its Nyquist plot around −1, together with the number of unstable open-loop poles, determines the number of unstable zeros of 1+L, which are the closed-loop poles.
